citation: Willatts DG, Reynolds F. Comparison of the vasoactivity of amide and ester local anaesthetics. An intradermal study. Br J Anaesth 1985;57:1006-1011
text_quality: ok (OCR of a two-column scan; body, both figure legends and the reference list are all present and legible). Two caveats: the columns are interleaved line by line, so no sentence longer than one printed line is contiguous in the text file; and the numeric data points of figures 1-4 are image only, so figure values were read from the rendered PDF page, not from the text.
design: Double-blind within-subject volunteer study of intradermal injection, run in two parts in one group of subjects. Part 1: amethocaine, lignocaine and prilocaine (three concentrations each) plus physiological saline. Part 2: procaine, cinchocaine and mepivacaine (three concentrations each) plus saline, in the same subjects. Solutions were randomly coded; the position of each solution varied randomly between subjects and was known to neither subject nor investigator. The saline control results from the two parts were combined. Analysis: Chi-squared with Yates' correction for proportions; GLIM3 linear modelling for the slope of log concentration v. duration of action per drug per subject, then one-way ANOVA on log-transformed slopes.
population: 10 fit adult volunteers (8 male), aged 21-40 years; one was an author, the others medical students or medical and laboratory colleagues. All gave informed consent.
n: 10 subjects, the same 10 in both parts. Each subject received a pair of injections of each solution, so n = 20 injections per drug-concentration and n = 40 for the saline control (the two parts combined); n = 10 subjects per point in figure 3.
setting: Anaesthetic Unit, St Thomas's Hospital Medical School, London. Healthy-volunteer laboratory study, 1985.
intervention: Six local anaesthetics as aqueous hydrochloride solutions, three concentrations each, each solution containing 0.1% sodium metabisulphite to stabilise the esters plus sodium chloride to render it isosmotic, autoclaved in randomly coded ampoules. Esters: procaine 0.1 / 0.3 / 1.0%; amethocaine 0.025 / 0.0833 / 0.25%. Amides: cinchocaine 0.01 / 0.033 / 0.1%; lignocaine 0.1 / 0.33 / 1.0%; racemic mepivacaine 0.1 / 0.33 / 1.0%; racemic prilocaine 0.1 / 0.33 / 1.0%. [Concentrations recorded here under the brief's exception, as what the study used.] No vasoconstrictor was added to any solution.
comparator: 0.9% sodium chloride 'control solution' carrying the same 0.1% sodium metabisulphite, injected in both parts of the study and the two sets of results combined.
route: Intradermal. A pair of 0.1-ml injections of each solution on the flexor surface of both forearms, spaced at 40-mm intervals. [Volume and spacing recorded here under the brief's exception, as what the study did.]
duration: Each injection followed to complete recovery. Colour was scored 5-10 min after injection; analgesia was tested from 10 min, every 5 min for the first hour and every 10 min thereafter until complete recovery. Complete recovery from all injections had occurred by 80 min. The per-drug duration endpoint was the time to 50% recovery.
outcomes: (1) Vasoactivity: local colour change classed pink / nil / pale at 5-10 min, plus any haemorrhagic change, expressed as percentage frequency (figure 1). (2) Analgesia: the central area of each bleb pricked 5 times with a lancet while the subject looked away, scored as the number of times out of 10 that the prick felt sharp; mean pinprick score as percentage recovery against time (figure 2). (3) Duration of action = time to 50% recovery, i.e. the time at which the sharpness score reached 5 out of 10, plotted per concentration in figure 3 and regressed on log concentration in figure 4.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Fairley JW, Reynolds F. An intradermal study of the local anaesthetic and vascular effects of the isomers of mepivacaine. Br J Anaesth 1981;53:1211-1216
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The 'only study' claim W-M001 rests on it. Willatts cites it for the contrary finding that L(+) mepivacaine's longer action was not associated with greater vasoconstriction. Willatts' own methods show the same half-recovery pinprick endpoint, so the two mepivacaine slopes are comparable quantities.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Aps C, Reynolds F. The effect of concentration on vasoactivity of bupivacaine and lignocaine. Br J Anaesth 1976;48:1171-1174
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The concentration/vasoconstriction trade-off this paper builds on. NOTE: Willatts' reference list prints this as 'Br. J. Anaesth., 48, 347', which is the Reynolds/Bryson/Nicholas aptocaine paper's page, not this one - a citation error in the 1985 paper.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Aps C, Reynolds F. An intradermal study of the local anaesthetic and vascular effects of the isomers of bupivacaine. Br J Clin Pharmacol 1978;6:63-68
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Source of the nil/pink/pale colour scoring and of the isomer vasoconstriction/duration link. NOTE: Willatts glosses its range as '0.48-3.84 mmol litre-1 (0.16-1.25%)'; the 1978 paper's own conversion makes 0.06-7.69 mmol/l equal 0.002-0.25%, so Willatts' percentage gloss is about tenfold too high.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Reynolds F, Bryson THL, Nicholas ADG. Intradermal study of a new local anaesthetic agent: aptocaine. Br J Anaesth 1976;48:347-354
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: A third human intradermal pinprick timing of mepivacaine and prilocaine, earlier than Fairley 1981. Bears on W-M001, W-M009 and D025: mepivacaine has been timed intradermally in human skin at least three times, not twice.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Padfield A. The intradermal local analgesic action of prilocaine. A controlled double-blind comparison with lignocaine and procaine. Anaesthesia 1967;22:556-561
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The other human intradermal timing of procaine. Willatts reports it as three plain solutions compared in volunteers, equi-analgesic shortly after injection, procaine shortest and prilocaine longest, with a 60% incidence of vasodilatation with procaine - and names no adrenaline arm, which bears on D023 and D054.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Foldes FF, McNall PG. 2-Chloroprocaine: a new local anesthetic agent. Anesthesiology 1952;13:287-296
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The single source for D023 and D054. Willatts quotes its intradermal content verbatim; this paper is the source-of-record for the second-hand quotation those pages carry.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Luduena FP. Duration of local anaesthesia. Ann Rev Pharmacol 1969;9:503
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Cited for the claim that the longer action of L(+) prilocaine, L(+) mepivacaine and L(-) bupivacaine over their isomers was solely attributable to greater vasoconstriction - the position Willatts' own dissociation result qualifies.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Altura BM, Altura BT. Effects of local anaesthetics, antihistamines and glucocorticoids on peripheral blood flow and vascular smooth muscle. Anesthesiology 1974;41:197
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Rabbit aortic strip work cited for procaine and amethocaine inhibiting agonist-induced contraction with potencies unrelated to anaesthetic potency; the animal counterpart to the dissociation finding.
